# Manojajātaka (Ja 397)

**ID:** Ja 397
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)

**Title (Pali):** Manojajātaka
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul6.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Manojajātaka* (Ja 397) is a birth story delivered by the Buddha while residing at the Bamboo Grove (Veḷuvana), occasioned by a monk who associated with bad company—an occasion noted as being shared with the *Mahilāmukha* birth tale [Fausböll 1883; Cowell 1897]. In the narrative of the past, the Bodhisatta was a lion living with his family in a mountain cave; his son Manoja provided game for the household, which included his parents, sister, and wife [Cowell 1897]. Manoja befriended an injured jackal named Giriya and disregarded his father’s counsel warning that jackals are immoral, sinful, and dangerous companions [Fausböll 1883; Cowell 1897]. Instigated by the jackal's desire to eat horseflesh, Manoja repeatedly preyed on the king's horses at the riverbank of Benares until a royal archer shot him with an arrow [Cowell 1897]. Hearing the bowstring, the jackal abandoned Manoja, declaring there is no friendship with the dying; Manoja managed to carry a dead horse to his den's mouth before collapsing dead, whereupon his kinsfolk recited stanzas on the perils of bad companionship [Cowell 1897]. In the *samodhāna*, the Buddha identified the treacherous jackal as Devadatta, Manoja as the monk led astray, the mother as Rāhulamātā, the sister as Uppalavaṇṇā, the wife as the nun Khemā, and the father as the Bodhisatta [Fausböll 1883; Nyanaponika et al. 2003].

Passage-level parallels for the verses on friendship are attested in the *Mitravarga* / Friendship chapters of the *Udānavarga* traditions (UV 25, UVS 25, Tibetan Uv Kg 25, and Chinese T 212.26 and T 213.25), alongside thematic connections with the *Sevitabbasutta* (AN 3.26) and *Jigucchitabbasutta* (AN 3.27). DharmaNexus corroborates these cross-language alignments with the Tibetan *Udānavarga* (D0326) and records Pali-internal reuse between the verses and their commentary in the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā*, as well as citations in the *Subodhālaṅkāraṭīkā* [DharmaNexus].
